Norfolk
NOR-fuk
n. (the East Anglian county of Norwich, which received the Dutch and Walloon stranger churches in 1565 and bred the first English separatism)
Old English Norþfolc, the north folk of the East Angles, as against the Suþfolc to the south.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Norfolk is the northern half of East Anglia, and in the sixteenth century Norwich was the second city of England. Two things fix the county in the dictionary. In 1565 the city invited a company of Dutch and Walloon refugees, driven out of the Low Countries by the Spanish persecution, to settle and work the new draperies; by the fifteen-eighties they were some four or five thousand in a city of sixteen thousand, worshipping in their own tongues in the Blackfriars and in Bishop Herbert's chapel under their own elders and deacons and a discipline of their own. They were the plainest example in England of a Reformed church fully ordered, and the English Puritans watched them closely. Secondly, Robert Browne gathered at Norwich about 1581 the first avowedly separatist congregation in England, on the principle that a true church is a company of believers covenanting together without waiting for the magistrate; he fled to Middelburg, recanted, and left behind a name for the whole tendency. Kett's rebellion had gathered on Mousehold Heath in 1549 and ended in slaughter. The dictionary records Norfolk as the county where England saw a Reformed church at work, and marks what it refused to learn from it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a stranger as a foreigner; a remnant as that which is left; an alien as one born in another country; a discipline as instruction and government; and a congregation as an assembly met for worship.

expand to see more

STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown; a guest.

REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.

ALIEN, n. A foreigner; one born in or belonging to another country; one not entitled to the privileges of a citizen.

DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to laws and rules; correction; chastisement.

CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of separate things; an assembly of persons met for the worship of God.

Key Scripture

Rom 11:5 — "Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace."

Isa 1:9 — "Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom, and we should have been like unto Gomorrah."

Zep 3:12 — "I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD."

Luk 12:32 — "Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom."

Modern Corruption

East Anglian county whose city of Norwich took in four or five thousand Dutch and Walloon refugees from 1565 and where Robert Browne gathered the first avowed separatist congregation about 1581.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's habitual method is a remnant, and that a remnant is usually poor and foreign-looking to the men among whom it is set. The strangers who came to Norwich were refugees with nothing but a trade and a church order; they were a quarter of the city within twenty years and they brought the new draperies with them. Paul states the doctrine as a present fact and not a consolation for bad times, that “at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5), and Isaiah says plainly what the alternative was, for “Except the LORD of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, we should have been as Sodom” (Isa 1:9).

The second thing to recover is the character God assigns such a company, and it rules out both the contempt the strangers often met and the pride a settled church takes in sheltering them. Zephaniah describes what the LORD leaves behind after judgment: “I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and poor people, and they shall trust in the name of the LORD” (Zep 3:12). Our Lord names His own people in the same register, “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luk 12:32). As to Browne, the dictionary holds that his principle was right and his practice unstable: a church is indeed a company covenanting in Christ and does not wait on a magistrate's leave, and a man who argues that and then conforms under pressure has not disproved the argument, only discredited himself. The strangers' churches, which had order and elders and stayed put, were the better model.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek leimma (G3005), a remnant; Hebrew sarid (H8300), a survivor; Greek poimnion (G4168), a flock.

expand to see more

Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant, that which is left over; “there is a remnant according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Greek ekloge (G1589) — a choosing out, election; “a remnant according to the election of grace”, Romans 11:5.

Hebrew sarid (H8300) — a survivor, one left remaining; “a very small remnant”, Isaiah 1:9.

Hebrew chasah-sense of taking refuge in Zephaniah's promise — “they shall trust in the name of the LORD”, Zephaniah 3:12.

Greek poimnion (G4168) — a little flock; “Fear not, little flock”, Luke 12:32.

Usage

"“there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5) — the strangers' churches at Norwich, 1565."

"“an afflicted and poor people” (Zep 3:12) — refugees with a trade and a church order."

"“Fear not, little flock” (Luk 12:32) — Browne's gathered congregation about 1581."
